opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a dramatic decision, and it wasn't because I thought OpenAI was a bad place. They have extraordinary people, and a lot of what defines this field came out of that building.

For me it came down to fit, and to what I wanted to learn at that stage. When you're choosing where to spend the next few years, you're really choosing a set of people, a research taste, and a way of making decisions. I asked myself which environment would push me to think most clearly about the problems I care about, and where I'd have room to work on things that weren't already obvious. My answer pointed somewhere else.

I also feel the culture of a lab matters more than people admit. How it treats safety, how it balances shipping with understanding, how much it lets individuals follow a hunch. Those things shape what you become as a researcher. I wanted a place whose instincts on those questions were closer to mine.

It's also not a forever choice. People move around in this field, and ideas move even faster. I don't see it as picking a side. It was a judgment about where I could grow and contribute most right now. I could be wrong, and I'm fine with that. It's the kind of mistake you learn from.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites fit, research direction, and lab culture as reasons for choosing elsewhere, but does not say he perceived too few people at OpenAI as steadily doing the work.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a bit more nuanced than "deciding against" OpenAI, because I was actually there for a while, and I learned a huge amount from the people and the culture. So maybe the more honest version of the question is why I didn't choose to stay, or why, when I had to decide where to spend the next several years, OpenAI wasn't the answer.

A few things went into it.

The first is about what kind of problem I wanted to work on. My whole research arc, from ReAct and Tree of Thoughts to SWE-bench and tau-bench, has been about language agents: models that act in environments, use tools, and get judged by whether they actually accomplish something. The pretraining phase of AI has largely been solved, and the frontier is now about environments, evaluation, and getting agents to do real work. Inside a large frontier lab, that work is very important but it's also one piece of a very big machine. I wanted to be in a position where the agent problem was the center of gravity, not one workstream among many.

The second is about degrees of freedom. At a place like OpenAI, the direction is set at a very high level and the organization is optimized for executing on that direction extremely well. That's a strength, and it's why they ship what they ship. But I'm still at a stage where I want to define the problem, not just solve a problem someone has already framed. I'd rather have a smaller team, a bit less compute, and a lot more ownership over what question we're even asking.

The third is more personal and, frankly, about China. I grew up there, I did my undergrad at Tsinghua, and I've watched the ecosystem change a lot over the last few years. There's a real chance to build something foundational on this side, with a different set of users, a different product surface, and different constraints that force you to think differently. I thought that if I didn't do it now, I'd regret it later. There was also a very simple human factor of wanting to be closer to family.

And the last piece is timing. In this field, the window where an individual researcher can meaningfully shape the trajectory of a technology is short. If I'd stayed, I would have been comfortable, and comfort was exactly the thing I was most worried about. So it wasn't a rejection of OpenAI as much as a bet on where I personally could create the most leverage.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites wanting agent research to be central, more ownership, building in China, family, and timing. It does not say his decision was primarily due to too few people at OpenAI steadily doing the work.
